content: Fermented milk products, also referred to as cultured dairy foods, cultured dairy products, or cultured milk products, are dairy-based foods that undergo fermentation with lactic acid bacteria. These bacteria include strains such as Lactobacillus, Lactococcus, and Leuconostoc. The fermentation process not only extends the shelf life of these products but also enhances their flavor and improves the digestibility of milk. Historical evidence suggests that fermented milk products have been produced as far back as 10,000 BC. Over time, various strains of Lactobacilli have been cultivated in laboratory settings, enabling the creation of a wide variety of cultured milk products with diverse flavors and characteristics. These products are found globally and include examples such as yogurt, cultured buttermilk, acidophilus milk, kiselo mlyako, sauermilch or dickmilch, zure melk, lapte bătut, filmjölk (commonly referred to as fil), surmelk or kulturmelk, piimä and viili, amasi (known as maas in Afrikaans), and doogh. Many types of cultured milk products are consumed in a manner similar to yogurt. They can be eaten from a bowl with a spoon, often paired with cereals, muesli, or cornflakes, or consumed as a beverage from a glass. Additionally, sugar and fruit flavors are frequently added to these products for commercial appeal. Cultured milk can also serve as an ingredient in various recipes. Certain variants of cultured milk contain live bacteria, which can stabilize the intestinal microbiota. Some of these products have been shown to offer health benefits. For instance, research by Seppo et al. (2003) demonstrated that milk cultured with Lactobacillus helveticus LBK-16H contains bioactive peptides, such as casokinins and lactokinins, which function as natural ACE inhibitors. These peptides exhibit antihypertensive properties, potentially contributing to cardiovascular health. It is also worth noting that Streptococcus lactis has been reclassified and is now known as Lactococcus lactis subsp.
